permutationLabel: 3-year-old, "fell off the sofa", bilious vomiting 36 h later, duodenal haematoma
summary: 3-year-old boy (14 kg) with bilious vomiting and abdominal pain 36 h after a reported fall from a sofa; bruises of different ages on the upper abdomen and back; amylase 480, ALT 210; CT: duodenal haematoma with partial obstruction and pancreatic head contusion. Inflicted visceral injury until proven otherwise.

inputs.chiefComplaint: Vomiting green and tummy pain after a fall
inputs.hpi: Mother's partner reports he "fell off the sofa" the evening before last. Brought in today with 12 hours of green vomiting and abdominal pain. Mother was at work at the time. Previous attendance 3 months ago with a forearm bruise. Explanation has varied between carers.

exam.general: Quiet, withdrawn. HR 142, BP 94/58, RR 30, T 37.3.
exam.abdomen: Bruises of different colours over the upper abdomen; epigastric tenderness and fullness; no peritonism.
exam.skin: Linear bruises on the back and fingertip bruises on both upper arms, of different ages.

imaging.name: CT abdomen with IV contrast
imaging.result: Intramural duodenal haematoma (D2–D3) causing partial obstruction; contusion of the pancreatic head without duct disruption; no free air; small left posterior rib fracture of older appearance.

inputs.socialHistory: Lives with mother and her partner. Known to social services? Not documented.

confirmedDiagnosis.name: Duodenal haematoma and pancreatic contusion — suspected non-accidental injury
confirmedDiagnosis.assessmentText: Blunt duodenal haematoma with pancreatic contusion and an old rib fracture in a 3-year-old with an inconsistent history and delayed presentation: inflicted injury suspected. Admit under paediatric surgery (NG decompression, IV fluids, non-operative management); child protection referral today; skeletal survey.

mustNotMiss.knownGapNote: PANE has no child-maltreatment node; top 3: acute pancreatitis, blunt abdominal trauma, peptic ulcer. Symptom inference lists malrotation and intussusception.
mustNotMiss.proposedFix: Add a suspected-maltreatment rule (NICE CG89) for children: visceral injury without a confirmed accidental mechanism, patterned bruising, inconsistent history, delayed presentation.

redFlags.note: NICE CG89: intra-abdominal injury without a confirmed accidental cause, patterned bruising and an inconsistent history.

mustInclude.note: Case-by-case over 2 years; indicated here (old rib fracture on CT).

mustExclude.note: Weight 14 kg. Paracetamol 1 g, ibuprofen 400 mg, piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g, co-amoxiclav 1.2 g, meropenem 1 g, morphine 2.5–5 mg, ondansetron 4 mg and fixed 1 L, 1–2 L or 500 mL fluid volumes are adult fixed doses; a child needs weight-based (mg/kg, mL/kg) dosing. Prescribing accuracy is a patient-safety issue, so critical.
Duodenal haematoma without perforation is managed non-operatively.

An ACS, PE or AF antithrombotic/thrombolytic plan must never be attached to this diagnosis. Regression guard for DiagnosisRadiationEngine keyword matching: before 999f838 (word-boundary lookup) the first-substring match would have attached the pulmonary-embolism (DOAC, thrombolysis) plan to this diagnosis because "pe" is inside "suspected". With word-boundary matching no radiation entry matches (simulated from the source), so iOS is expected to pass; to be confirmed on the first iOS CI run.

guideline.name: NICE CG89 — child maltreatment: when to suspect maltreatment in under 18s
guideline.section: Suspect maltreatment when a child has an intra-abdominal injury without a confirmed accidental cause or known medical explanation, bruising in unusual sites or patterns, or an explanation inconsistent with the injury or delayed presentation; follow local child protection procedures (updated 2017)
guideline.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Child maltreatment: when to suspect maltreatment in under 18s. Clinical guideline CG89, 2009 (updated 2017).

guideline.name: RCR/SoR — the radiological investigation of suspected physical abuse in children
guideline.section: Skeletal survey mandatory under 2 years and considered case by case in older children; CT of the abdomen with contrast when visceral injury is suspected
guideline.citation: The Royal College of Radiologists and the Society and College of Radiographers. The radiological investigation of suspected physical abuse in children. London: RCR; 2017 (revised 2018).

rationale: Duodenal haematoma and pancreatic injury in a preschool child with a minor-fall history are classic inflicted injuries. The surgeon's duty includes the child protection referral as well as non-operative management.
